tldr: The minimax actual welfare regret for exact population-feasible treatment allocation is \(n^{-3\beta/(4\beta+4)}\), without a logarithmic factor, over the entire stipulated fixed-radius H\"older neighborhood of a quartic contact. A legal ridge family with a single compensation shared by every sign configuration proves the original Bernoulli-record lower bound against all admissible randomized binary selectors. A finite observable population-Gram projection and equal-area ranking attain the rate, with mass exactly \(q\) on every dataset. The same rate holds on the natural superclass of bounded \(C^{2,\eta}\) benefits with public derivative and Hessian H\"older bounds and \(\partial_{xx}\tau_u\ge m_0\). The numerical exponent agrees with square-root-margin smooth classification and fixed-level weighted-loss machinery; the certificate proves it for the endogenous fixed-mass cutoff on these specific causal law classes. There is no fixed-radius elbow. No shrinking-radius or geometry-indexed phase theorem is claimed.
gap: \cite{KitagawaTetenov2018,AtheyWager2021} bound best-in-class regret, and known-law exact population capacity is already permitted. The separation proposition exhibits the omitted approximation loss on an overlapping constrained linear class. \cite{ZhouAtheyWager2023} credits asymptotically minimax multi-action learning with restrictions; \cite{Pellatt2026} supplies general-resource regret and cost oracle inequalities. These results inform the question, without a claimed strict rate comparison. A matching lower experiment inside the fixed uniform-law, ridge-containing Hölder neighborhood must preserve its endogenous population cutoff; a lower bound over a broader law class does not establish that result.
fill: A total public-Gram projection and equal-area allocation supply exact every-dataset feasibility. Paired perturbations with one shared compensation provide a concrete lower-testing handle. The full-class question requires matching original-record regret against all randomized jointly Borel selectors, with finite-sample and compact-uniform constants.
